title: Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a room-temperature processor that runs general-purpose programs while recovering much of the electrical energy normally lost during switching. It would combine logically reversible computation, which preserves information instead of routinely erasing intermediate results, with physically adiabatic operation, which changes circuit states in a controlled way that allows signal energy to return to the power supply. Its defining achievement would be substantial energy savings for completed programs across the whole system at useful throughput.

Logical reversibility and adiabatic operation are distinct requirements. Preserving information avoids the thermodynamic cost associated with erasure, but does not by itself recover switching energy or eliminate physical losses. Conversely, demonstrating adiabatic energy recovery in a circuit does not establish that its computation is logically reversible. Earley's theoretical analysis derives a rate-dependent dissipation bound under its physical assumptions: finite-rate reversible computation still has a cost. That bound is not a measurement showing that every implementation's dissipation increases monotonically with clock speed.

significance.text: If the processor achieved large wall-plug savings at comparable useful throughput, it would deliver substantially more computation within a fixed power budget and release less heat per completed task. That would matter for both power-limited edge devices and large computing installations. Earley's analysis supplies a theoretical basis for an asymptotic advantage over irreversible computation under stated resource-scaling assumptions; it does not establish the size of a practical processor's advantage or predict commercial success.

Engineering synthesis: lower heat could relax thermal constraints on packaging and permit more useful computation in a given volume. Greater usable density would also depend on memory, interconnects, power delivery and fabrication. Software support, manufacturing yield and the energy costs of moving and storing data would determine whether an efficient switching mechanism became an efficient general-purpose platform.

The supplied research attributes to Frank and Edwards' 2025 industry perspective a forecast of only about a twofold improvement in conventional CMOS gate-level efficiency over the following dozen years, together with an argument that miniaturization alone cannot overcome reliable field-effect switching constraints. No source text for that article was retained for the supplied review, so these remain attributed claims rather than established premises of this record. The concept's potential importance does not depend on accepting that particular forecast.

The thermodynamic comparison needs care. The familiar kT ln 2 erasure cost is not a universal minimum energy expenditure for every reversible operation. Approaching that value is also not synonymous with dissipationless computation. A finite-rate bound must be interpreted with its physical assumptions and operation definition; it neither promises arbitrarily small dissipation at arbitrary speed nor, by itself, settles every comparison with kT ln 2.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated room-temperature general-purpose processor whose information-preserving logic and physical energy recovery produce a large, measured whole-system advantage at useful speed. The supplied evidence documents relevant theory and a dated cryogenic processor demonstration, but does not establish this room-temperature capability or determine whether it remains unmet as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering synthesis: energy recovery must survive the losses of real devices, wiring, clock distribution and power conversion. Charge must be transferred and recovered with sufficiently little resistance, leakage and timing error, while states remain reliable in room-temperature thermal noise. Running more slowly may reduce some adiabatic losses, but can sacrifice throughput and increase the contribution of losses accumulated over time. The challenge is an advantageous operating point for a complete machine, rather than a low-energy transition considered in isolation.

Engineering synthesis: general-purpose execution also requires managing intermediate information, memory updates, branching, data movement and external input and output. Reversible execution must preserve or deliberately dispose of information without allowing storage growth, cleanup work or irreversible interfaces to consume the recovered energy. Memory, control, software and error management must work together within the same energy budget. These are proposed integration barriers, not separately demonstrated impossibility results.

current_state.text: Hannah Earley's A Universal Constraint on Computational Rates in Physical Systems, supplied as arXiv version 2 dated October 23, 2022, develops an open-system analysis of the entropy cost of reversible computation at finite temperature. The supplied review had a complete, identity-verified paper and found support for erasure-cost avoidance and a rate-dependent adiabatic lower bound. The paper also discusses fast-switching departures from a strict linear relationship. It is theoretical work supplied as an arXiv preprint, not a processor demonstration; the inputs do not establish a subsequent peer-reviewed publication.

The April 2021 MANA paper reports a 4-bit adiabatic superconducting microprocessor operated at 4.2 K. Full-processor operation was demonstrated at 100 kHz, including two short programs of four instructions each. A separate execution-stage chip was demonstrated up to 2.5 GHz. These results establish a limited adiabatic processing demonstration at cryogenic temperature; the execution-stage speed must not be presented as the demonstrated full-processor rate. Evidence of adiabatic operation alone also does not establish logically reversible computation.

The supplied research additionally attributes to MANA an energy figure of 1.4 zJ per Josephson junction at a 5 GHz clock design point. The detailed supplied review does not establish that figure's measurement basis or full accounting boundary, so it is retained here as an attributed device-level figure requiring clarification. It is not a measured wall-plug energy per completed processor operation. MANA's estimates for practical cryosystems are projections, distinct from its measured chip results.

The IEEE HTML extraction for MANA contained no source text, but a separately supplied complete PDF was identity- and content-verified in the review and supports the historical demonstrations described above. The unusable HTML extraction therefore does not invalidate those results. This record relies on that supplied review and does not imply a new inspection of the paper or its waveform figures.

The supplied research describes a September 3, 2025 EE Times report of company measurements on a Vaire 22 nm test chip, with reported energy-recovery factors of 1.77 for a capacitor array and 1.41 for a shift register. Neither the article text nor a supporting artifact was available to the supplied review, so those values, their definitions and their measurement boundaries remain unverified here. Even if confirmed, component recovery factors would not establish a 100-fold improvement for a general-purpose processor at the wall plug. The inputs do not establish independent replication; that limitation is not evidence that the reported measurements are false.

The supplied research dates Frank and Edwards' CMOS industry perspective to September 29, 2025 and attributes to it a conventional switching-energy limit likely in the thousands of kT, alongside its roughly twofold efficiency forecast. Because no article content was retained for review, the quantitative baseline and the detailed field-effect switching argument cannot be confirmed from the supplied evidence. They should not be used as a numerical starting point for judging completion.

Evidence boundary: no freshness searches were supplied. These dated theoretical and hardware results therefore do not establish the complete hardware frontier on November 1, 2026. In particular, the categorical claim that no room-temperature processor has demonstrated large wall-plug gains on real programs cannot be sustained from these inputs. The record also contains no verified demonstration of the full proposed capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed engineering criterion: demonstrate a foundry-fabricated processor operating at room temperature that executes nontrivial general-purpose programs with at least 100 times lower measured wall-plug energy per completed useful operation than a specified conventional CMOS baseline at comparable useful throughput. Sustain full-chip operation at megahertz-class clock rates or higher, while reporting useful completed operations per second separately from clock frequency. The 100-fold and megahertz thresholds are proposed choices, not published standards or demonstrated feasibility claims.
completion_criteria.label: Foundry room-temperature megahertz processor, 100-fold lower wall-plug energy than CMOS

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement boundary: include power conversion, energy-recovery clock generation and distribution, memory, control and input/output within explicitly matched system boundaries. Specify workloads, numerical precision, output correctness, error rates, operating temperature, memory capacity and throughput. Report total task energy as well as energy per defined operation so that additional reversible instructions or cleanup work cannot create a misleading advantage through the operation count.
completion_criteria.label: Matched system boundaries reporting total task energy and per-operation energy

completion_criteria.text: Characterize measured energy per defined information operation over a range of rates and compare it with an applicable adiabatic model whose assumptions and parameters are stated. Demonstrate logical information preservation separately from physical energy recovery. Earley's analysis motivates the finite-rate comparison, but supplies neither a universal numerical target at megahertz rates nor the candidate's proposed performance thresholds. Neither dissipationless operation at arbitrary speed nor convergence to kT ln 2 is required.
completion_criteria.label: Energy across rates versus stated adiabatic model, preservation separate from recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criterion: publish enough circuit, software, workload and measurement detail for independent replication, and repeat the advantage across multiple chips and a varied program suite. Establish the practical operating envelope, including load, rate, memory and reliability limits. Finite testing would demonstrate breadth across the tested conditions; it would not prove literal universality or an energy advantage for every program.
completion_criteria.label: Replication detail, multi-chip program-suite advantage, and operating envelope

completion_criteria.text: A resonator-only or component-only energy-recovery experiment would not satisfy this processor-level proposal. MANA's 4-bit, 4.2 K demonstration would also not qualify because it does not meet the room-temperature scope, regardless of its value as evidence for adiabatic computing. Neither component recovery nor projected system performance can substitute for a measured, matched whole-system comparison.
completion_criteria.label: Measured matched whole-system comparison of a room-temperature processor

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, has the closest technical overlap. Superconducting adiabatic circuits can be relevant to energy recovery, and MANA illustrates the cryogenic branch of that work. CPE-02 requires room-temperature general-purpose recovery of switching energy; CPE-06 targets a superconducting classical system whose total wall-plug advantage must accommodate cooling. These remain separate targets. Only CPE-06's roster title and the supplied research characterization are available, so its detailed scope and internal overlap treatment cannot be verified.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, addresses a complementary source of energy cost. Efficient switching alone does not establish that moving data has ceased to dominate a workload. CPE-04, Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory, instead specifies an optical computing and storage platform. Either could share efficiency goals with CPE-02, but neither roster title establishes logical reversibility or adiabatic energy recovery.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-05, Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy, targets learning capability and biological-scale energy performance rather than a general-purpose reversible processor. CPE-08, Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer, targets density, manufacturability and defect tolerance. Advances in either might complement CPE-02, but their completion would not establish its thermodynamic operating principle or whole-system energy advantage.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-01, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, concerns quantum computation with error correction, while CPE-07, Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet, concerns quantum networking. Reversibility is relevant to the theory of quantum operations, but CPE-02 is a classical computing target and requires neither quantum application advantage nor a quantum network. All three entries retain distinct identities.

The supplied research identifies historical item 3 with CPE-02, but the historical entry itself was not supplied, so that identity cannot be independently reconciled here. Its reported wording about dissipation arbitrarily close to kT ln 2 for arbitrary computation needs context: the erasure scale, reversible-operation dissipation and finite-rate constraints are different quantities. The historical wording should not be treated as a demonstrated result or as this record's completion criterion.

unresolved_issues: Whether any room-temperature general-purpose processor has demonstrated substantial matched wall-plug savings by November 1, 2026 remains undetermined because no freshness searches were supplied.
The full text of the 2025 CMOS perspective is needed to assess its switching-floor argument, thousands-of-kT estimate and roughly twofold efficiency forecast.
The Vaire report's recovery-factor definitions, measurement boundaries, operating conditions and independent replication remain unverified in the supplied review.

The MANA 1.4 zJ figure requires clarification of its measurement or estimation basis, operation definition and relationship to the 5 GHz design point; it is not established here as whole-system energy.
The practicality of the proposed 100-fold advantage at megahertz-class full-chip rates remains unestablished, and a reproducible baseline and workload suite would need specification.
Historical item 3 and the full CPE-06 entry are needed to verify the asserted historical identity and detailed cross-entry overlap.

No substantive review recommendation was rejected. Unverified quantitative research details were retained as explicitly attributed claims to preserve useful information without presenting them as validated results.

brief.title: A computer that recovers energy while it works
possible: You could run everyday programs on a room-temperature computer that recovers much of the electrical energy its circuits normally lose as heat. It would preserve intermediate information and return switching energy to the power supply while completing useful work at a practical speed.
why: Small devices with tight power budgets and large computing installations could do more work with the same electricity. Less heat per completed task could also ease cooling and packaging constraints.

sources.showed: An industry perspective on conventional chip efficiency limits and the case for computing that preserves information and recovers electrical energy.
sources.cited_for: It supplies an argument for pursuing alternatives to conventional switching.
sources.not_established: An industry perspective does not demonstrate a processor's energy advantage.

sources.showed: This theoretical preprint derives a lower limit on heat production during information-preserving computation under stated physical assumptions. The limit depends on computing speed.
sources.quote:
That is, the per-operation dissipation scales in-
versely with delay.
sources.cited_for: Preserving information avoids erasure costs but does not eliminate heat production at useful speed.
sources.not_established: The theory does not establish the energy savings of a practical processor.

sources.showed: A report of company measurements of energy recovery in test-chip components.
sources.cited_for: It describes component-level work toward recovering switching energy.
sources.not_established: Component recovery does not establish whole-computer savings on completed programs.

sources.who: Christopher L. Ayala and colleagues, Yokohama National University
sources.showed: The team demonstrated MANA, a small processor using controlled switching to recover energy, at extremely low temperature. A separate chip tested its execution units at higher speed.
sources.quote:
We also successfully demonstrated a high-
speed breakout chip of the microprocessor execution units up to
2.5 GHz.
sources.cited_for: MANA demonstrates processing and memory functions using energy-recovering circuits.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate room-temperature operation, information-preserving computation or measured whole-system energy savings.

shown: Ayala and colleagues demonstrated the complete MANA processor at 100 kHz, running short programs at extremely low temperature. Its faster execution-unit test was a separate demonstration.

Earley's theoretical preprint explains why preserving information still leaves a speed-dependent heat cost under its assumptions. Neither that theory nor MANA establishes the proposed room-temperature computer's whole-system advantage.
missing: A room-temperature processor must combine information preservation and energy recovery while running substantial programs at useful speed.
Savings must survive memory access, data movement, power conversion and the work of managing intermediate information.
Matched measurements must establish total electricity savings across varied programs, with independent replication.

milestones.label: A factory-made processor with large electricity savings
milestones.explanation: A factory-made room-temperature processor would have to run substantial programs with a megahertz-class clock and 100-fold lower outlet energy at matched useful speed. This tests practical savings; megahertz means millions of ticks per second.

milestones.label: Complete accounting of energy for finished tasks
milestones.explanation: Matched tests would have to count power supplies, clocks, memory, control and input/output, reporting task energy and energy per defined operation. This prevents extra instructions or cleanup work from disguising costs.

milestones.label: Measured speed costs and separate proof of information preservation
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to compare energy across speeds with a stated model of controlled energy recovery, and separately demonstrate information preservation. This distinguishes the mechanisms and tests their physical costs.

milestones.label: Repeatable savings across chips and varied programs
milestones.explanation: Published details would have to enable independent replication, with savings repeated across chips and programs and practical limits measured. This establishes how broadly the advantage holds.

milestones.label: A measured comparison of complete room-temperature computers
milestones.explanation: A matched comparison would have to measure a complete room-temperature processor's electricity use. This establishes whether component energy recovery becomes a whole-system advantage.

uncertain: Whether the proposed hundredfold savings can coexist with useful full-processor speed remains open.
The conventional comparison computer and program suite still need specification.
The best balance between slower switching, accumulated losses and reliable room-temperature operation remains unresolved.

page.title: Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer
page.definition: A room-temperature general-purpose computer uses logic in which the complete state after each step uniquely identifies the permitted state before it. A power clock times the logic and gradually charges and discharges its circuits, recovering electrical energy for reuse. The complete computer uses less energy per completed program than a corresponding irreversible computer at the same throughput. Existing adiabatic processors such as the 8-bit nRERL recover switching energy while allowing some operations to discard information.

goal.need: Data centres used an estimated 485 TWh of electricity worldwide in 2025. Conventional processors dissipate switching energy as heat. Smaller switches can reduce that loss, but erasing information still carries a heat cost. Preserving information and reusing switching energy could let operators run more parallel work within the same power budget. The saving depends on how much energy the clock recovers and how much extra work and storage the program needs.

figures.caption: IEA estimates for worldwide data-centre electricity consumption in 2024.
figures.note: Facility consumption includes computing equipment and supporting infrastructure; these figures do not estimate recoverable switching energy.

completion.title: A room-temperature reversible computer uses less whole-system energy at matched program throughput.
completion.criterion: A general-purpose hardware computer operates at room temperature, approximately 300 K, using information-preserving logic and energy-recovering power clocks. For every program in a disclosed suite, it consumes less total electrical input energy than a specified irreversible reference at matched correct-output throughput and numerical precision; the difference exceeds measurement uncertainty. Energy includes power conversion, clock generation and distribution, memory, control, input/output, cooling, and restoration of reusable working storage. The comparison covers completed tasks, including the work needed to make their execution reversible.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no accessible outside acceptance test was found for the complete capability.
completion.basis: IRDS identifies savings after power-clock losses as the goal. Searches of IRDS, IEEE Rebooting Computing reports, DARPA programmes and Vaire documents found no accessible acceptance test for this complete capability. This fallback therefore requires a positive measured advantage without choosing a gain factor or clock rate. Earley's preprint, revised on 23 October 2022, derives a rate-dependent dissipation bound under its assumptions, not a processor acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: A fabricated circuit maps distinct allowed input states to distinct complete output states.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated circuit maps each permitted input state to a distinct complete output state. The output, including any retained auxiliary information, uniquely identifies the input.
milestones.set_by: Reversible-computing community; the logical reversibility criterion formalised by Frank and Shukla, 2021, sections 2.1.3–2.1.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Reversible computational operations include only one-to-one transitions such as (a).

milestones.title: A reversible logic circuit and its power clock achieve an energy-recovery factor greater than 1.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated reversible logic circuit operated with its energy-recovering power clock achieves an energy-recovery factor Rf greater than 1. Rf is the logic energy divided by the energy dissipated per cycle, including losses in the power clock.
milestones.set_by: Vaire's Ice River proof-of-concept test, described by its CTO on 3 September 2025; its technology whitepaper defines the zero-recovery boundary at Rf = 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: For a traditional system with an R-factor of 1, efficiency is 0: no energy is recovered.

milestones.title: A room-temperature processor runs reversible programs with reversible circuits and an energy-recovering clock.
milestones.criterion: At room temperature, an integrated processor executes stored reversible programs that exercise arithmetic, memory access and branching. Reversible circuits implement the instruction set, and the power clock recovers switching energy during execution.
milestones.set_by: MIT Reversible Computing Project; Vieri's 1999 thesis, section 2.1, states the required integration of supply, circuits, architecture and programs. Applied here within the room-temperature scope.
milestones.threshold_quote: Reversible electronic computers must have a reversible power supply, which power reversible circuits, which implement a reversible architecture, which runs reversible programs.

milestones.title: A 64-bit adiabatic adder uses at most 1% of the power of an equivalent CMOS adder.
milestones.criterion: A 64-bit adder built from adiabatic circuits operates at no more than 1% of the power of an equivalent adder built with CMOS technology current at the time of the demonstration.
milestones.set_by: Second IEEE Rebooting Computing Summit, Working Group on Adiabatic and Reversible Computing, Appendix F

1% of the equivalent circuit constructed using
then-current CMOS.

milestones.title: An adiabatic processor delivers 1 GFLOPS at no more than 1% of equivalent CMOS processor power.
milestones.criterion: An adiabatic processor delivers one billion floating-point operations per second while using no more than 1% of the power of an equivalent circuit built with CMOS technology current at the time of the demonstration.
milestones.set_by: Second IEEE Rebooting Computing Summit, Working Group on Adiabatic and Reversible Computing, Appendix F
